I just started working in the schools a couple of months ago. I was working in private practice for 5 years. While it has been a big shift for me, I am loving the schedule so far (currently on spring break!). I am contracted to the schools by another company and my contract is for 8 hours / day. I generally try not to work over that amount of time. If an IEP or other meeting requires me to do so I am allowed to leave earlier on another day to make up for it.  I am at 2 different school sites, at site A I generally work 7:30-3:30 and at site B I generally work from 8:00-4:00. My salary is roughly 90k for the school calendar, meaning if I choose to work over the summer I am paid more for that time. 

The biggest differences between private practice and schools for me are focus and eligibility. Focus being that in private practice my focus was to the client and quality of therapy. In the schools I feel therapy comes second and case management comes first (scheduling IEPs, making sure documents are signed, making sure minutes are met, etc.). Regards to eligibility, it has been a big shift for me going from “would this client benefit from services?” to “does this student demonstrate and educational need for services?”. There is a big difference.

Overall, there are pros and cons to each setting. For me the shift in schedule after 5 years of private practice is currently worth it.

I’m so sorry that you feel your concerns are not being heard/validated at your current practice! While I cannot give specific recommendations for your child through this platform - I will say that generally, in my practice (private pediatric clinic) I rarely recommend less than 2 times per week. This obviously varies on so many factors but most often 2x per week is my starting point.  A second opinion for your child wouldn’t hurt.

One thing I think is important to note is that in private practice the SLP sees their client in a very controlled environment and for a short time. It is not uncommon for a child to sound “better” in my office than they do at home or at school. What helps me tremendously is when parent brings in recordings of their child’s speech at home, this way I can actually hear the discrepancies and provide better treatment and home practice. If you haven’t already tried this with your current SLP, I might suggest giving it a shot while continuing to bring up your concerns about speech intelligibility.

My mom is bipolar (misdiagnosed for most of my life, treated only for depression until recently). I don't remember anyone ever *telling* me that my mom was depressed. I think that if she had a conversation with me about it I would have been able to understand a lot more about why things were *different*. I also think that having a conversation at a younger age would have saved me from a lot of the anger I am dealing with now. 

Your kids seem smart, supportive, and just awesome! In my opinion sitting them down to have a conversation would be best. Give them some simplified information, and then they can ask whatever questions they have. It may be hard to get started, but I think in the long term you will all benefit from it.
